prompt: On a legacy 100BASE-TX link, a server is forced to 100 Mbit/s full duplex while the switch detects the speed but uses half duplex. The link is up. Which symptoms are consistent with this duplex mismatch under bidirectional load?

options.text: The switch port logs late collisions
options.explanation: Possible. The half-duplex side detects overlapping transmissions, which can include late collisions depending on timing.

options.text: The server's NIC counts CRC errors and runt frames
options.explanation: Possible. Aborted/truncated transmissions from the half-duplex side can cause FCS/alignment or fragment counters; exact counter classification varies.

options.text: Pings succeed but large transfers are very slow
options.explanation: Possible. Light traffic may avoid overlap, while heavier bidirectional traffic exposes the mismatch.

options.text: The link fails to come up at all
options.explanation: The question explicitly states that this mismatched legacy link is up. Other negotiation/configuration failures can prevent links coming up.

workedExample: The full-duplex side can transmit while receiving. The half-duplex side treats overlapping transmissions as collisions and backs off. Error counters and heavy-load performance can reveal the mismatch even when small pings pass. Align supported settings, normally auto-negotiation on both ends; this legacy 100BASE-TX scenario does not describe every Gigabit PHY.

prompt: Suppose you tried to run gigabit Ethernet in half duplex with CSMA/CD and the normal 64-byte minimum frame, and no carrier extension. Signals travel at about 2 × 10⁸ m/s. Ignoring repeater and electronics delays, roughly how far apart could the two most distant hosts be?

options.text: About 2.5 km, the same as 10 Mbit/s Ethernet
options.explanation: 2.5 km is not the result of this propagation-only hypothetical. The calculation gives 51.2 m; historical Ethernet topology limits also include equipment delays.
That's the round-trip distance the signal can cover in 0.512 µs. The hosts must be half that apart, because the signal goes there and back.
Correct. The 512-bit slot takes 0.512 µs at 1 Gbit/s, in which a signal covers 102 m. A round trip of 102 m means at most about 51 m end to end.
This is off by a factor of ten, perhaps from using 10 Gbit/s timings. At 1 Gbit/s a bit lasts 1 ns.

workedExample:
The rule: the sender must still be transmitting when news of a collision at the far end gets back.

```formula
t_slot = 512 bit / (10⁹ bit/s)
t_slot = 0.512 µs
D_rt = v × t_slot
D_rt = 2 × 10⁸ m/s × 0.512 × 10⁻⁶ s
D_rt = 102.4 m
d_max = D_rt / 2 ≈ 51 m
where
t_slot: the time to send the minimum 512-bit (64-byte) frame at 1 Gbit/s
bit: one binary digit; bit/s is bits per second
s: seconds
µs: microseconds, millionths of a second
D_rt: the round-trip distance a signal covers while that frame is being sent
v: the signal speed in the cable, about 2 × 10⁸ metres per second (m/s)
m: metres
d_max: the largest possible distance between the two hosts
≈: approximately equal to
In words: a signal covers 102.4 m during one minimum frame, and it has to go there and back, so the hosts can be at most about **51 m** apart.
```

Real equipment delays would shrink this further. Historical half-duplex Gigabit used a 4096-bit-time slot with non-data carrier-extension symbols after short frames. These symbols do not turn the MAC payload into a 512-byte frame. Modern full-duplex operation avoids this collision-domain constraint.

prompt: On a 10 Mbit/s shared Ethernet, a frame has just suffered its **third** collision. Using binary exponential backoff, what is the maximum randomly selected backoff interval, excluding additional carrier-sense deferral?

options.explanation: This is 3 slots, treating the collision count as the maximum K. After the third collision the random slot count is drawn from 0 to 2³ − 1 = 7, not from 0 to 3.
Correct. After the 3rd collision the random slot count is chosen from 0 to 2³ − 1 = 7. The maximum wait is 7 × 512 bit-times = 7 × 51.2 µs = 358.4 µs.
This waits 8 slots (2³). After the third collision the range is 0 to 2³ − 1, so the largest wait is 7 slots.
That is the cap for retries after collisions 10 through 15 (K up to 1023, about 52.4 ms). A frame is abandoned after the sixteenth failed attempt.

workedExample:
```formula
K ∈ {0, 1, …, 2^{min(n, 10)} − 1}
n = 3: K ∈ {0, 1, …, 7}
t_slot = 512 × 0.1 µs = 51.2 µs
t_max = 7 × t_slot = 358.4 µs
where
K: the number of slot times to wait, chosen at random
∈: "is one of": K is picked from the set in braces
…: and every whole number in between
n: the number of collisions this frame has had, 3 here
min: the minimum, the smaller of the two values (caps the range after 10 collisions)
t_slot: one slot time: 512 bit-times; at 10 Mbit/s one bit lasts 0.1 µs
µs: microseconds, millionths of a second
t_max: the longest possible random backoff
In words: after the third collision the host waits 0 to 7 slots of 51.2 µs, so at most **358.4 µs**.
```

The doubling makes the expected wait grow quickly with congestion: with many hosts colliding, the range soon becomes wide enough that one of them is likely to pick a unique, lowest value and win.
